newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU fertility rate falls to postwar low in 1995.
newsitem.headline: EU fertility rate falls to postwar low in 1995.

text.p: The European Union's fertility rate fell to a postwar low in 1995, with fewer than four million babies -- or 1.43 per woman -- born in the 15 member states, EU statistics office Eurostat said on Monday.
Migration accounted for 75 percent of the EU's population increase last year, also a postwar record, Eurostat said in statement No 63/96.

The EU's population on January 1, 1996 stood at 372,662,100 -- up 0.3 percent over the previous year. The natural increase -- births minus deaths -- was 290,100, while net immigration increased the population by 800,000.

The report showed that Germany and Italy would have lost population without migration. "Germany had a natural decrease of 115,500 and a net immigration of 421,900, overwhelmingly the Union's highest flow," the statement said.
"Italy showed a similar pattern with a natural decrease of 32,100 and a gain due to migration of 94,000."
The only countries to record a net outflow of migrants were Ireland and Portugal.
However, the net inflow of migrants to the EU fell from a peak of 1.3 million in 1992 to 800,000 in 1995.
Ireland had the EU's highest fertility rate in 1995, with 1.87 children per woman, followed by Finland at 1.81, Denmark at 1.8 and Sweden at 1.74, the statement said.
The lowest rates were in Italy, with 1.17, and Spain with 1.18. Germany had a fertility rate of 1.24, France of 1.7 and Britain of 1.71.
The EU's natural population growth in 1995, less than 300,000, compared with 1.6 million in the United States, 15.7 million in India, almost 12.5 million in China and 303,000 in Japan.

The report said that EU life expectancy at birth fell slightly in 1995 to 80.1 years for women and 73.7 years for men. French baby girls can expect to live the longest -- to 81.9 years, while Sweden has the longest life expectancy for boys -- 76.1 years.
